design_detail: Systematic review without meta-analysis (PRISMA-guided; no protocol or registration reported) of how 'set' (participant selection, preparation, integration) and 'setting' (monitors, environment, end of session) were described in clinical trials of classic psychedelics in people with psychiatric disorders other than substance use disorders. PubMed and Web of Science to 12 September 2022, rerun on 6 December 2023, plus reference lists; English or French. 27 articles on 25 trials (13 randomized, 12 open-label) of psilocybin (16), ayahuasca (5), LSD (2) and 'DMT' (2, one of which is a 5-MeO-DMT formulation); 761 participants by the Results (763 in the abstract). Each trial was scored for whether it reported 16 predefined sub-domains (Table 2) and its practices were described (Table 3); the trials were not appraised and their outcomes were not synthesized.
can_establish: What 25 published clinical trials of classic psychedelics for psychiatric disorders (to December 2023) reported about participant selection, preparation, monitors, environment, music and end-of-session procedures, and how completely they reported it.
cannot_establish: Whether any element of set or setting changes therapeutic outcomes or the risk of a difficult experience (no included trial compared settings, the trials were not appraised and no outcomes were synthesized); what trials did but did not report (the score measures reporting); and practice outside clinical trials, in healthy volunteers, in addiction treatment, or with MDMA or ketamine, all of which were excluded.

sample.recruitment: Database search of PubMed and Web of Science (drug names LSD, psilocybin, ayahuasca, N,N-dimethyltryptamine, ibogaine or mescaline, combined with setting, therapeutics, psychotherapy or psychiatry) to 12 September 2022, rerun with the same strategy on 6 December 2023, plus manual search of reference lists (PDF p. 2, Methods › Data source and research strategy). Figure 1 (PDF p. 3): 3,045 PubMed and 1,867 Web of Science records (4,912); 1,282 removed for lacking an English or French abstract, 3,322 on title and 71 as duplicates; 237 abstracts screened, 47 full texts assessed, 15 articles included, and 12 more added after the update.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: peer-reviewed clinical trials in English or French, with a title and abstract, in participants with a psychiatric diagnosis. Excluded: reviews, meta-analyses and expert opinion; healthy volunteers (47 at abstract stage); addiction treatment and withdrawal; articles on the population of an already included study without a new or modified protocol (23 at full text); MDMA and ketamine, as not classic psychedelics (PDF pp. 2–3, 17).
sample.demographics: Trial sizes 6 to 233; one trial (Goodwin et al., 2022) contributes 233 of the 761 participants (31%, editors' arithmetic). 12 of 25 trials in the USA only, all ayahuasca trials in Brazil. Mainly depression: 8 trials in major depressive episodes, 2 recurrent, 5 treatment-resistant, 6 depression or anxiety with a life-threatening illness; one each in OCD, social anxiety, body dysmorphic disorder, anorexia nervosa and bipolar II depression (PDF p. 4; Table 1, pp. 5–6). Women 422 of 761 (55%) by the editors' sum of Table 1.
sample.selection_effects: Trials only, of classic psychedelics, in psychiatric patients without substance use disorders; two databases, English or French, no registries or grey literature. Trial participants were heavily screened: 13 trials excluded anyone with occasional or regular use of an illicit psychoactive substance other than alcohol, 7 a history of alcohol dependence, and the ayahuasca trials anyone who had taken ayahuasca before (once in four trials, twice in one); two trials allowed no more than 10 previous hallucinogen experiences, and one required previous tolerated use of an indole psychedelic (PDF p. 7). Features were scored as reported in articles, supplements and protocols, so a practice done but not described counts as absent.

exposure.measurement: Presence or absence of 16 set-and-setting sub-domains as described in each trial's article, supplements and protocols, scored out of 16 per trial, plus a narrative description of each trial's practices (Tables 2 and 3). Who did the scoring, and whether it was checked by a second reviewer, is not stated.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Trial doses are listed in Table 1 as trial conditions (PDF pp. 5–6) and are not reproduced here. Session length in Table 3 ranges from 2 h (intravenous DMT) to 12 h (LSD), mostly 6–8 h for psilocybin and 4 h for ayahuasca (PDF pp. 11–15).
exposure.polysubstance: Trial rules on medicines and other substances before sessions, as listed by the review (PDF p. 7, Results › Drug interactions; numbers of trials are the editors' tally of the studies cited): washout of antidepressants and other psychotropic medicines, most often at least 2 weeks before the first dose (13 trials), with other schedules elsewhere; no cannabis for 24 h before each session (4 trials); alcohol and other psychoactive drugs strongly discouraged for 24 h before each session (3 trials) or stopped for 2 weeks during full-time hospitalization (3 ayahuasca reports); no food supplements in the week before (2 trials); no tyramine-rich foods for 24 h before and 12 h after ayahuasca because of its monoamine-oxidase-inhibiting content (1 trial); caffeine withheld for 24 h (1 trial) or taken as usual on the morning (2 trials); no nicotine from 2 h before until questionnaires about 7 h after psilocybin (1 trial). None of these rules was evaluated.

comparison.controls: Not applicable: no included trial compared settings; the review compares how completely trials reported each feature.

outcomes.instruments: Six predefined domains, refined into 16 sub-domains during full-text reading: participant selection (general health, drug interactions, exclusion criteria); pre-session interventions (information on effects, therapeutic-alliance meeting, advice on the attitude to adopt); post-session meeting; monitors (specific training, presence and number during the session, prior meeting with the participant); environment (pleasant environment, safe environment, control of visual distractors, control of sound distractors); end of session (debriefing, safe return home) (PDF pp. 2–3; Table 2, p. 10).
outcomes.validity_norms: The domains were based on earlier publications, including safety guidelines for hallucinogen research (Johnson et al., 2008) and Carhart-Harris et al. (2018); no validation or inter-rater reliability of the score is reported.
outcomes.operationalization: A sub-domain counts as present if the trial described it anywhere in its article, supplement or protocol; no description counts as missing. The total out of 16 measures completeness of reporting, not quality of practice or any effect on outcomes.

analysis.effect_sizes: No effect sizes. Number of the 25 trials reporting each sub-domain (Table 2, PDF p. 10): general health, drug interactions and exclusion criteria 25 (100%) each; information on effects 21 (84%); therapeutic-alliance meeting 19 (76%); advice on attitude 18 (72%); post-session meeting 20 (80%); specific monitor training 13 (52%); monitor present during the session 18 (72%); prior meeting of monitors and participant 18 (72%); pleasant environment 17 (68%); safe environment printed as 20 (80%), although the column has 21 ticks (84%; editors' count on the rendered page and the text layer); control of visual distractors 16 (64%); control of sound distractors 19 (76%); debriefing 19 (76%); safe return home 20 (80%). Median total 14 of 16, range 6 to 16; 3 trials reported all 16 (PDF pp. 16, 18).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned; the 16 sub-domains were refined during full-text reading (PDF p. 2).
analysis.selective_reporting: Figure 1 gives the flow of the first search only; the December 2023 update, which supplied 12 of the 27 articles, has no flow numbers. No list of excluded studies.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Across 25 trials (27 articles) to December 2023, every trial reported health screening, checks for drug interactions and exclusion criteria, while reporting of other set-and-setting features varied: monitor training 52%, visual distractors 64%, pleasant environment 68%, advice on attitude 72%, monitor present 72%, therapeutic-alliance meeting 76%, sound control 76%, debriefing 76%, post-session meeting 80%, safe return home 80%, information on effects 84% (Table 2). The median trial reported 14 of 16 features; only 3 reported all 16. No included trial compared different sets or settings.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract's conclusion, that differences in set and setting limit comparability and reproducibility and that harmonization would help, is supported. The discussion goes further: that therapeutic effects in trials with minimal set and setting "suggests that psychedelics have a therapeutic effect independently of the context" (PDF p. 17). The trials cited for this (three ayahuasca reports and two labelled DMT) are all open-label without a control group, were not appraised, and scored low on a measure of reporting rather than practice (the authors themselves think missing training information is a reporting omission, p. 17); no included trial varied context. The same paragraph then suggests that set and setting optimized for mystical-type experiences might give a better effect, which no included trial tested, and the Results state that a two-interview preparatory phase maximized the experience and the therapeutic effects in one trial (p. 8), although preparation was not varied there. The abstract's figures also differ from the Results (763 vs 761 participants; psilocybin 47%, against 16 of 25 trials).

timeline.event: Carhart-Harris et al., perspective on the importance of context: one of the publications used to predefine the review's domains (PDF p. 2).
Kaelen et al., 'The hidden therapist': cited in the discussion as the one study relating the subjective experience of music to the psychedelic experience (PDF p. 17).
Haijen et al., prospective study cited in the discussion as agreeing that emotional breakthrough and mystical experience predict lower depression scores (PDF p. 17).

Strickland et al.: randomized comparison of two music genres during psilocybin sessions in a smoking-cessation pilot (n = 10), a comparison of settings that falls outside this review's scope because addiction trials were excluded.

Golden et al., rapid scoping review of setting with wider designs (healthy volunteers, naturalistic and quasi-experimental studies): none of its 29 empirical studies overlaps with this review's (PDF p. 18).
Seybert et al., systematic review scoring psychedelic trials against the TIDieR reporting checklist, cited as using a similar method (PDF p. 18).

replication.where_it_stands: A systematic map of set-and-setting reporting in psychiatric trials of classic psychedelics to December 2023. It shows inconsistent reporting and no trial comparing settings; evidence that particular elements matter remains correlational within trials (therapeutic alliance in Murphy et al., 2022, and music in Kaelen et al., 2018, as the review cites them), plus one small randomized comparison of music genre in an addiction trial outside its scope (Strickland et al., 2021). Its participant total may count some ayahuasca participants more than once (see reporting issues).

funding.funder: The authors received no financial support for the research, authorship and/or publication of the article (PDF p. 18).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declared no potential conflicts of interest (PDF p. 18).
funding.affiliations_note: Department of Psychiatry, CHU Nîmes and University of Montpellier; CH Thuir; Department of Biostatistics (BESPIM), CHU Nîmes; University of Santiago de Compostela; CIBERSAM, Madrid (PDF p. 1). None of the review's authors appears among the listed authors of the included trials in the reference list.

what_would_settle_it: Randomized trials that vary one element of set or setting at a time (for example music or none, one or two monitors, a decorated or a standard room, more or less preparation) under otherwise identical psychedelic treatment, with registered outcomes including difficult experiences; and a reporting standard for psychedelic trials (a TIDieR extension or a Delphi consensus, as the authors propose) so that reviews can compare what trials actually did.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (people with a psychiatric disorder, substance use disorders excluded), intervention (a classic psychedelic in a clinical trial) and outcome (16 set-and-setting sub-domains) are specified; no comparator is needed for the descriptive aim.
No protocol or registration is mentioned, and the sub-domains were refined during full-text reading (PDF p. 2).
Restriction to peer-reviewed clinical trials is explained (to prioritize robust designs), and its cost, the exclusion of more experimental designs, is acknowledged (PDF p. 18).

Two databases with the keywords given and reference lists searched, and the exclusion of grey literature is justified; but the English-or-French limit is not justified (1,282 records were dropped at the first step for lacking an English or French abstract), and there was no registry search or expert contact. A close call with partial yes, which requires justified publication restrictions.

Titles and abstracts of the first search were screened independently by two reviewers, but the update, which supplied 12 of the 27 articles, was screened by one reviewer and cross-checked by another (PDF pp. 2, 18).
Study characteristics were collected by one of two reviewers; who scored the 16 sub-domains, and whether the scoring was checked, is not stated (PDF p. 2).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Reasons are counted in Figure 1 for the first search only; no list of excluded full texts.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 1 gives country, drug, dose, indication, sex split, design and sessions, adverse effects and main outcome for each trial, and Table 3 gives detailed set-and-setting practice.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: No risk-of-bias or quality appraisal of the trials; the 16-item score measures completeness of reporting, not bias.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported

domains.note: No data synthesis was planned, given the descriptive aim (PDF p. 4).

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The discussion infers a therapeutic effect independent of context from five open-label, uncontrolled ayahuasca and DMT reports without considering their risk of bias (PDF p. 17).

Variation in practice, the review's outcome, is described and discussed (two approaches to the room, fewer monitors in recent trials, less developed set and setting in ayahuasca and DMT trials); no outcome results were synthesized, so there is no outcome heterogeneity to explain.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: No conflicts and no funding declared (PDF p. 18).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: AMSTAR 2 applies because this is a systematic review by design, although the tool was built for reviews of effects and this review maps reported practice. Five critical items are not met (no protocol, a restricted search, no list of excluded studies, no appraisal of the trials, risk of bias ignored when inferring an effect), which gives critically low confidence. Practically: the counts of what the 25 trials reported can be checked against Tables 2 and 3 (one column total is off by one) and can be cited as a description of these published trials and of how inconsistently set and setting are reported; they cannot be cited for what trials in general did, for whether any element of set or setting changes outcomes (no included trial compared settings and none was appraised), or for the authors' inference that psychedelics work independently of context.

key_findings.finding: Search and selection: 4,912 records from PubMed (3,045) and Web of Science (1,867) to 12 September 2022; after removing 1,282 without an English or French abstract, 3,322 on title and 71 duplicates, 237 abstracts were screened and 47 full texts assessed; 15 articles were included, and the December 2023 update added 12 (no flow numbers given), for 27 articles on 25 trials.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Data source and research strategy (p. 2); Figure 1 (p. 3); Results › Study selection (p. 4)
key_findings.note: The database counts (3,045 and 1,867) and the exclusions by step (1,282, 3,322, 71) are printed only in Figure 1, an image without a text layer; read on the rendered page. The Results text gives 4,912, 4,675 removed, 237, 190, 32, 15 and 12.

key_findings.finding: The 25 trials: 13 randomized (6 against placebo, 2 against an active comparator or active placebo, 1 against a waiting list, 4 comparing doses) and 12 open-label; 16 psilocybin, 5 ayahuasca, 2 LSD and 2 labelled DMT; sizes 6 to 233, 761 participants; 12 in the USA only, all ayahuasca trials in Brazil; five trials reported at least one serious adverse event, from hypotension and bradycardia to suicidal ideation in 5 participants.
key_findings.locator: Results › Characteristics of the studies, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 1 (pp. 5–6)
key_findings.note: One of the two trials labelled DMT (Reckweg et al., 2023) is a vaporized 5-MeO-DMT formulation according to its title in the reference list (p. 20). The abstract gives 763 participants.

key_findings.finding: Participants' drug histories in the trials: 13 trials excluded anyone with occasional or regular use of an illicit psychoactive substance other than alcohol, 7 excluded a history of alcohol dependence, the ayahuasca trials excluded previous ayahuasca use, two trials allowed no more than 10 previous hallucinogen experiences, and one (Moreno et al., 2006) required previous well-tolerated use of an indole psychedelic.
key_findings.locator: Results › Selection process for participants, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Trial rules before sessions, as listed: antidepressant and other psychotropic washout, most often at least 2 weeks before the first dose (13 trials); no cannabis for 24 h before each session (4 trials); alcohol and other psychoactive drugs strongly discouraged for 24 h before (3 trials); no food supplements in the preceding week (2 trials); no tyramine-rich food for 24 h before and 12 h after ayahuasca because of its monoamine-oxidase inhibitor content (1 trial); caffeine withheld for 24 h (1 trial) or taken as usual (2 trials); no nicotine from 2 h before until about 7 h after psilocybin (1 trial). None of these rules was evaluated.
key_findings.note: The review lists the studies for each rule without counting them; the numbers of trials are the editors' tally of the studies it cites (the 13 for the 2-week washout counts Carhart-Harris et al., 2021, and Murphy et al., 2022, as one trial).

key_findings.finding: Preparation: information on effects was given in 21 trials and not mentioned in 4; in 19 trials clinicians met participants beforehand to build trust, in one to four meetings of about 2 h each on days other than the session (6–8 h in all in one trial); advice on attitude centred on openness and letting go; two trials (three articles) used a structured approach based on acceptance and commitment therapy; in 4 trials participants visited the session room beforehand.
key_findings.note: The text lists three studies for the acceptance-and-commitment approach, but two of them (Carhart-Harris et al., 2021; Murphy et al., 2022) are articles on one trial.

key_findings.finding: Monitors: training was described in 13 trials (52%), often only as specific training; 12 trials kept two monitors in the room throughout and one had four; five trials published in 2023 used a single monitor per participant; some trials stressed male–female monitor pairs, while others rejected them.
key_findings.locator: Results › Monitor training and presence during the session, 2nd paragraph (p. 9); Table 2 (p. 10); Discussion, 6th paragraph (p. 17)

key_findings.finding: Environment and music: trials either disguised the hospital room (living-room style, decorated, flowers or plants; sofa, recliner or bed) or left the hospital setting unchanged (4 trials); 11 trials asked participants to wear an eye mask throughout and 1 to close their eyes; 16 played a predefined playlist through headphones and one alternated music and silence without headphones; two trials allowed no music (dos Santos et al., 2021, music and films not allowed; D'Souza et al., 2022, no music and no decoration). The authors judge the choice between disguising and decorating the room to have been made arbitrarily, without evidence.
key_findings.locator: Results › Session environment, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 9); Table 3, dos Santos and D'Souza rows (p. 13); Discussion, 5th paragraph (p. 17)

key_findings.finding: Food on session days, as recorded in Table 3 and never evaluated: a light or low-fat breakfast or a light snack (Moreno 2006, Grob 2011, Griffiths 2016, Palhano-Fontes 2019, Davis 2021, Sloshower 2023); a light meal and fruit or light snacks available during the session (Goodwin 2022, Lewis 2023); a meal provided (Reckweg 2023, timing not stated) or shared with therapists and family at the end of the session (Aaronson 2023); and, in the anorexia nervosa trial, a standardized breakfast introduced partway through the study to avoid hypoglycaemia (Peck 2023).

End of session: an end-of-session debrief in 9 trials according to the text (19 in Table 2); 24 h of in-hospital observation in 6 trials; 12 trials ensured that participants did not drive within 24 h (staying in hospital, a taxi, or collection by a relative or close person), and one required a phone call on arrival home.

Completeness: median 14 of 16 sub-domains reported (range 6 to 16), only 3 trials reported all 16, and reporting was least complete for monitor training (52%), control of visual distractors (64%) and a pleasant environment (68%); ayahuasca and DMT trials scored lowest (6 to 12 in Table 2).
key_findings.locator: Table 2 (p. 10); Results › Overall quality of description of set and setting domains and sub-domains in the studies (p. 16); Discussion, 7th paragraph (starts on p. 17; the passage on all 16 items is on p. 18)

key_findings.finding: The authors found no study comparing the efficacy of psychedelics in different sets and settings and state that it is unclear how important context is for a therapeutic effect.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives 763 participants; the Results give 761, which matches the editors' sum of Table 1.

The abstract says psilocybin was over-represented at 47%, but psilocybin trials are 16 of 25 (64%) and contribute 596 of 761 participants (78%; editors' arithmetic from Table 1); no basis for 47% is given.
reporting_issues.consequence: Do not cite 47%; it may be a figure left from the first set of 15 articles, but the paper does not say.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says the databases were searched until 12 December 2023, while the Methods give 12 September 2022 for the first search and 6 December 2023 for the update.

In Table 2 the column 'care to create a safe environment' has 21 ticks (all trials except Schneier 2023, Holze 2023, Goodwin 2023 and Reckweg 2023) but its total is printed as 20 (80%). The 25 row totals, which agree with their ticks, sum to 314, one more than the sum of the printed column totals (313).
reporting_issues.consequence: Editors' count, confirmed on the rendered page and on the text layer: 21 of 25 (84%). The abstract's statement that a safe environment was consistently present rests on this column.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says an end-of-session debrief was organized in nine trials (p. 16), while Table 2 counts debriefing in 19 (76%) (p. 10).
reporting_issues.consequence: The two counts probably use different definitions (Table 2 may include discharge assessments), but the paper does not explain; cite either only with its definition.

reporting_issues.issue: The text states that all studies were conducted in a hospital facility (p. 9), but Table 3 describes one trial in a room in a private practice office (Gasser et al., 2014, p. 11) and one in an outpatient office (Sloshower et al., 2023, p. 14).
reporting_issues.consequence: Not every included trial took place in a hospital.

reporting_issues.issue: Reckweg et al. (2023) is counted as a DMT trial (text and Table 1), but its title in the reference list describes a vaporized 5-methoxy-N,N-dimethyltryptamine formulation (GH001), that is 5-MeO-DMT.
reporting_issues.consequence: Only one trial (D'Souza et al., 2022) concerns DMT itself; the 5-MeO-DMT trial belongs to a different drug page.

reporting_issues.issue: Three ayahuasca reports use the same single-dose protocol in the same Brazilian inpatient setting: Osório et al. (2015, titled a preliminary report), Sanches et al. (2016) and Zeifman et al. (2021, titled results from an open-label trial); Zeifman's row has the same sex split as Sanches's (14 women, 3 men) and refers to Sanches for adverse effects. The review counts them as three trials and adds their participants, without saying whether they overlap, although it excluded 23 other articles for reporting an already included population.
reporting_issues.consequence: If the Osório and Zeifman samples are within Sanches's, up to 23 of the 761 participants are counted twice and the ayahuasca evidence comes from three trials, not five; not settled by the review.

reporting_issues.issue: The discussion attributes both a survey of nearly 2000 people who had used psilocybin mushrooms (11% reporting that they had put themselves or others at significant physical risk) and an adverse event rate under 1% among 250 trial participants to the same reference, Carbonaro et al. (2016), which the reference list gives as a survey of challenging experiences after psilocybin mushrooms.
reporting_issues.consequence: The source of the trial figure cannot be identified from this review; do not cite it from here.

reporting_issues.issue: Smaller text–table mismatches: the discussion says almost two-thirds of trials described post-session interviews (p. 18), but Table 2 gives 20 of 25 (80%); it says most trials insisted on male–female monitor pairs (p. 17), while the Results say monitor gender was only occasionally specified (p. 9); the text's list of 16 psilocybin trials names Lewis 2023a and 2023b separately and omits Aaronson 2023, which Table 1 lists as a psilocybin trial (p. 4); the text speaks of 27 included studies where it means articles (p. 4).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the tables, not the discussion's summaries, should be cited for counts.
